c.v: In 2024 the Michigan State Police recorded 35,951 crashes in Oakland County, 9,139 people injured, 509 of them seriously, and 68 killed, the second-highest crash count of any Michigan county. The county’s claims look different from Wayne County’s. Drivers here more often carry real liability coverage, so the fight is less often about an uninsured driver and more often about whether a $100,000 or $250,000 policy is enough for a serious injury, and whether the client’s own underinsured motorist coverage makes up the difference. The roads are the Road Commission for Oakland County’s, not a city’s. And the case is heard in Pontiac, in the Sixth Circuit, whose practices differ from Detroit’s.

sections.heading: Who pays after an Oakland County crash

c.v: Your no-fault (PIP) claim, against your own insurer.

Under MCL 500.3107, your own policy pays medical expenses up to the PIP level you selected ($250,000, $500,000, or unlimited for most Oakland County policyholders; $50,000 is available only to Medicaid enrollees), 85 percent of lost wages for up to three years (capped at $7,201 a month for crashes in the year beginning October 1, 2025), replacement services at $20 a day, and attendant care, regardless of fault. If you have no policy, a spouse’s or resident relative’s policy pays (MCL 500.3114), and if none exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3172), capped at $250,000 for medical benefits. Written notice must reach the insurer within
one year
(MCL 500.3145(1)); each bill must be paid within 30 days of reasonable proof or carry 12 percent interest (MCL 500.3142). Our
no-fault insurance claim page
covers the application, the benefits, and the denials.
Your claim against the at-fault driver.

For pain and suffering and economic losses beyond no-fault, you need a threshold injury under MCL 500.3135: death, serious impairment of body function, or permanent serious disfigurement. The deadline is three years (MCL 600.5805(2)). Recovery is reduced by your share of fault and barred above 50 percent (MCL 500.3135(2)(b), 600.2959). For vehicle damage, the
mini tort
under 3135(3)(e) recovers up to $3,000 from the at-fault driver for your deductible or unpaid repair cost.

sections.heading: What makes an Oakland County crash claim different

c.v: The policy limits question.

The insurance available after an Oakland County crash depends on the policies involved, including the at-fault driver’s liability limits, the injured person’s PIP coverage, and any uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage.

That changes the shape of a serious-injury claim. Michigan’s minimum liability coverage is $50,000 per person and $100,000 per crash (MCL 500.3009(1)), with a default of $250,000/$500,000 unless the buyer chose less; some at-fault drivers carry $250,000 or more. When the injury exceeds the at-fault driver’s limit, the client’s own
underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage

pays the difference up to the UIM limit, under the policy’s conditions, which typically require the insurer’s consent before the client settles with the at-fault driver. Getting that consent, and the order in which the liability and UIM claims are resolved, is a recurring Oakland County problem. See our
uninsured and underinsured motorist page
The road is the Road Commission’s.

Oakland County’s county roads, which include most of the mile roads and arterials that are not state trunklines, are maintained by the Road Commission for Oakland County (RCOC), a separate agency. A crash caused by a qualifying defect in the improved portion of a county road may support a claim against the RCOC under the highway exception to governmental immunity, MCL 691.1402, with written notice generally required within 120 days under MCL 691.1404. Claims based solely on defective or malfunctioning traffic signals generally do not fall within that highway exception.). State trunklines (I-75, I-696, M-59, Telegraph, Woodward, and parts of Orchard Lake Road) are under MDOT jurisdiction. Qualifying state highway-defect claims generally require notice within 120 days under MCL 691.1404, filed with the Court of Claims as prescribed by statute;); city streets belong to the 62 municipalities. The RCOC also maintains a countywide traffic-signal network. Claims involving signal timing or sight-distance conditions require separate analysis of governmental immunity, road conditions, and the applicable legal duties.
Government vehicles.

SMART buses, school buses from the county’s 28 districts, municipal police and fire vehicles, and RCOC trucks and plows. A crash involving one of these government-owned vehicles may support a claim under the Governmental Tort Liability Act’s motor vehicle exception, MCL 691.1405, when the injury results from negligent operation of the vehicle. Separate notice requirements may apply; certain tort claims against SMART, for example, require written notice within 60 days under MCL 124.419. See our
bus accident page
The case will be in the Sixth Circuit.

Most Oakland County injury suits over $25,000 are filed in the Sixth Judicial Circuit Court at 1200 N. Telegraph Road in Pontiac. Mini tort and other small claims go to the district court for the community: the 46th in Southfield, the 47th in Farmington Hills, the 48th in Bloomfield, the 44th in Royal Oak, the 50th in Pontiac, the 51st in Waterford, and the 52nd District’s four divisions in Novi, Clarkston, Rochester Hills, and Troy, among them. Venue is determined under the statutory order of priority in MCL 600.1629, generally beginning with the county where the original injury occurred and where a defendant resides, conducts business, or maintains a registered office. Other counties may be appropriate if the higher-priority statutory criteria are not met.
Where you were treated.

Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital in Royal Oak, the county’s Level I trauma center, Corewell Health Troy and Farmington Hills, Henry Ford West Bloomfield, McLaren Oakland and Trinity Health Oakland in Pontiac, Henry Ford Providence Southfield Hospital and Henry Ford Providence Novi Hospital, and DMC Huron Valley-Sinai in Commerce are among the hospitals treating Oakland County crash patients. faqs.question: How many car accidents happen in Oakland County each year?

answer.v: 35,951 in 2024, with 9,139 people injured and 68 killed, according to the Michigan State Police, about 12 percent of Michigan’s crashes.

faqs.question: The other driver’s insurance offered their policy limit. Should I take it?

answer.v: Not before checking your own underinsured motorist coverage and getting your insurer’s written consent to settle. Accepting the liability limit without consent can forfeit the UIM claim under most policies. A lawyer can sequence the two claims so you recover both.

faqs.question: I was hurt because of a bad signal or pothole on a mile road in Oakland County. Who is responsible?

answer.v: A qualifying defect in the roadway may support a claim against the Road Commission for Oakland County, with written notice generally required within 120 days under MCL 691.1404. A malfunctioning traffic signal is different because governmental immunity generally protects the agency from claims based solely on signal maintenance. If the road was a state trunkline such as Telegraph, Woodward, or M-59, a qualifying highway-defect claim against MDOT generally requires notice within 120 days, filed with the Court of Claims.

faqs.question: Where would my Oakland County car accident case be filed?

answer.v: Most injury suits go to the Sixth Judicial Circuit Court in Pontiac. Mini tort and other claims under $25,000 go to the district court for the community where the crash occurred or the defendant lives.

Your own no-fault insurer, regardless of fault, up to your PIP level, after you file an Application for No-Fault Benefits within one year; a household member’s insurer if you have none; the Assigned Claims Plan if no policy applies.
One year to give your no-fault insurer written notice, three years to sue the at-fault driver, and as little as 120 days for a claim against the RCOC or a city.

faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer for a minor crash in Oakland County?

answer.v: Not if no one was hurt and the insurer is paying. Call if anyone was injured, the other driver’s limits may be too low for the injury, a government vehicle or road defect was involved, the police report is wrong, or an insurer has denied or delayed benefits.
